title: The seamless robe (John 19:17–24)
hook: soldiers gamble for his coat, woven in one piece

segments.voice: Yesterday, thorns and purple, and Pilate's ecce homo. Your line was behold the man. Who did you really look at? Day six hundred forty-six.

Executions in the Roman world had a grim little economy. The soldiers on duty kept what the condemned man left behind. Sandals, a belt, a cloak. At the foot of the cross, four soldiers are dividing up Jesus's clothes. They split them into four shares, one each. And then they come to one piece they don't want to cut. The Gospels don't linger on the nails. John lingers on this: a garment, and a game of chance.

First, John sets the scene. Jesus goes out "bearing his cross" to the place of a skull, in Hebrew, Golgotha. He's crucified between two others. Pilate has a sign fixed above him, Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews, written in Hebrew, Greek and Latin, so anyone passing can read it. The chief priests ask him to change it to he said he was king. Pilate refuses: "What I have written I have written." Then the clothes. In the King James Bible: "now the coat was without seam, woven from the top throughout." Woven in one piece, top to bottom, no stitching. The soldiers say, let's not tear it; let's cast lots for it. And John says this fulfilled a line of the Psalms: "They parted my raiment among them, and for my vesture they did cast lots." That's Psalm twenty-two, a psalm that begins in anguish and ends in praise, and Christians have long read it alongside the crucifixion. Why does John care about a robe? He doesn't say. Readers have offered answers for centuries. The first-century historian Josephus describes the high priest's tunic as woven in one piece, so some readers see Jesus here as a priest. Early church writers, like Cyprian of Carthage in the third century, saw the robe as a picture of the church: one piece, which even the soldiers wouldn't tear. And some just see the cruel ordinariness of it: men gambling at the foot of a cross while a man dies above them. All three can sit together. The text simply gives us the robe, and leaves it with us.
screen: `WHAT I HAVE WRITTEN I HAVE WRITTEN.`

`PRIEST, CHURCH, OR A GAMBLE AT A CROSS?`
then, large: `WOVEN FROM THE TOP THROUGHOUT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give away a piece of clothing. Settle, and breathe. Picture your closet or your drawers. Somewhere in there is something warm and good that you haven't worn in a year. A coat, a sweater, a pair of shoes. Picture it, and picture someone who could use it this week: a shelter, a coat drive, a neighbor, a friend's kid. Let yourself feel the little tug of not wanting to let go. Then let it go, in your mind first. If you pray, you can offer it as a small gift. The bell holds the time.
The seamless robe. Jesus's coat, woven in one piece from the top, which the soldiers wouldn't tear, and gambled for instead.
Your line: woven from the top. Today, actually bag up the piece of clothing you pictured, and put it by the door so it leaves the house. Day six hundred forty-six.

howItsDone: Christians remember the dividing of Jesus's garments in the Stations of the Cross, and in many churches on Maundy Thursday the altar is stripped bare, which some link with this scene.

original.note: Greek: seamless, without stitching. it appears only here in the New Testament.

what it means: soldiers gamble for a coat they won't tear, and John hears Psalm 22 in it.
what a scholar hears: araphos, used only here in the New Testament. Josephus says the high priest's tunic was woven in one piece, and Cyprian read the robe as the church's unity.

notes: Roman custom of executioners taking the condemned's clothing: commonly stated in commentaries. Confirm.
Josephus, Antiquities 3.7.4 (3.161): the high priest's tunic not of two pieces but woven as one. Confirm reference.
Cyprian, De unitate ecclesiae 7: the seamless robe as the unity of the church. Confirm section.
araphos occurs only at John 19:23 in the NT. Confirm.
